concepts.name: Checking that an LLM judge can be trusted
Percentiles vs the average for latency
Excessive agency and its three root causes
Defending an agent against indirect prompt injection

questions.prompt: A domain expert labelled 200 traces, and 10 of them are failures. Your new LLM judge marks all 200 as Pass. Which statement is right?

choices.text: It agrees with the expert 5% of the time, because it never says Fail
It agrees 95% of the time, which is good enough to gate pull requests
Its agreement can't be computed until the judge outputs 1–5 scores
It agrees 95% of the time but catches none of the 10 failures

questions.explanation: It matches the expert on the 190 passing traces, so 190 / 200 = 95% agreement, yet it detects 0 of the 10 failures. Hamel Husain uses this example to show why raw agreement misleads when failures are rare. Measure separately the share of real failures the judge catches and the share of good outputs it passes.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "How do you know your LLM judge is trustworthy?" Describe how you would check it.

model_answer.summary: Treat the judge as a classifier and measure it against a domain expert's labels. Tune its prompt on some labelled examples and measure it once on examples it has never seen.
key_points: A domain expert labels real traces Pass or Fail, with a short critique, and those labels are the ground truth
Labelled examples are split: a few go in the judge's prompt, a dev set is used to improve the prompt, and a held-out test set is used once at the end
Report the share of real failures the judge catches and the share of good outputs it passes (TPR and TNR), not raw agreement
Binary Pass/Fail labels are preferred to 1–5 scales, because the gap between a 3 and a 4 is subjective
Generic off-the-shelf metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore, cosine similarity) don't show that a judge agrees with your expert

questions.explanation: The judge is only as good as its agreement with the person whose standard it stands in for. Keeping a test set the prompt was never tuned on keeps the reported numbers honest. Tracking both rates matters because catching more failures can cost more false alarms.

questions.prompt: Why do Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar recommend binary Pass/Fail labels over a 1–5 scale for LLM evals?

choices.text: A binary call forces a clear decision; 3 vs 4 is subjective and inconsistent between labellers
LLM judges can't reliably output numbers, so a scale always fails to parse
Binary labels halve the number of tokens each judge call uses
A 1–5 score can't be averaged across traces, so trends are invisible

questions.explanation: Their evals FAQ says binary evaluations force clearer thinking and more consistent labelling, while the difference between adjacent scale points is subjective and varies between annotators. A middle score also tells nobody what to fix. Scores can be averaged; the problem is that they don't mean the same thing to every labeller.

questions.prompt: Your agent sends `POST /v1/charges` to a payments API, and the connection drops before any response arrives. What makes a retry safe?

choices.text: Resend it as `PUT`, because `PUT` is idempotent
Retry with the same `Idempotency-Key` header, so the server returns the first request's saved result
Retry with a new idempotency key each time, so the server treats it as a fresh request
Retry only on a `500`, because a `500` means nothing was charged

questions.explanation: `POST` isn't idempotent, so a blind retry can charge twice. With an idempotency key the server saves the status code and body of the first request for that key, and returns them for every repeat with the same key. A new key per attempt defeats this. Changing the method doesn't make the endpoint idempotent. And a `500` doesn't prove nothing happened: Stripe even replays a saved `500` for the same key.

questions.prompt: With Stripe's API, a retry reuses an idempotency key, but its body has a different `amount` from the first request. What does Stripe do?

choices.text: Creates a second charge for the new amount
Returns the first request's result and ignores the new amount
Returns an error, because the parameters don't match the original request
Updates the first charge to the new amount

questions.explanation: Stripe's docs say the idempotency layer compares incoming parameters with the original request's and returns an error if they differ, to prevent accidental misuse. A key names one operation. Reusing it for a different operation is a bug in the client. This is Stripe's behaviour; other APIs that take idempotency keys may differ.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "How do you safely retry a call that is not idempotent?" Use an agent tool that sends an invoice as your example.

model_answer.summary: Give each logical operation a unique idempotency key and send the same key on every retry. The server stores the result under that key and returns it for repeats instead of running the operation again.
key_points: `POST` is not idempotent, unlike `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT` and `DELETE` (RFC 9110), so a blind retry can send the invoice twice
The client generates one unique key per operation (for example a UUIDv4) before the first attempt and reuses it on every retry
The server saves the first result for the key and returns it for later requests with the same key
A request that reuses a key with different parameters is rejected, not treated as a new operation
Keys expire (Stripe prunes them after at least 24 hours), so retries must happen inside that window

questions.explanation: The key must be created once per operation, not once per HTTP attempt, or every retry looks new. Store it with the agent's step, so a worker that crashes and restarts sends the same key.

questions.prompt: Out of 100 agent requests, 94 take 100 ms and 6 take 2,000 ms. Using the nearest-rank method (p95 is the 95th of the 100 sorted values), what are the mean and the p95?

choices.text: Mean 214 ms, p95 100 ms
Mean 1,050 ms, p95 2,000 ms
Mean 214 ms, p95 2,000 ms
Mean 100 ms, p95 214 ms

questions.explanation: Mean = (94 × 100 + 6 × 2,000) / 100 = (9,400 + 12,000) / 100 = 214 ms, a latency no request actually had. Sorted, values 1–94 are 100 ms and values 95–100 are 2,000 ms, so the 95th value is 2,000 ms. The p95 shows the slow tail the average hides. The 1,050 ms answer averages the two distinct values instead of all 100 requests.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "Why is p95 more useful than the average?" Answer for an agent's response latency.

model_answer.summary: Latency is a distribution with a long tail, and an average hides both the tail and changes in it. A high percentile tells you what the slowest users actually experience.
key_points: Latency is a distribution, not a single number, and a few very slow requests form a long tail
A simple average can hide tail latency, and changes in it
p95 = X means 5% of requests are slower than X, so it describes real users' worst experience
Use p50 for the typical case and p95 or p99 for a plausible worst case, and set targets on them

questions.explanation: Google's SRE book gives an example where a typical request takes about 50 ms but 5% of requests are 20 times slower, which the average hides. Agents make the tail worse, because a few runs take many more tool-call steps or produce much longer outputs.

questions.prompt: An inbox-summary agent uses a mail tool that can read, send and delete, with a full-mailbox OAuth scope. By OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency, what is the problem, and what is the fix?

choices.text: Hallucination; lower the temperature so the model doesn't invent actions
Excessive autonomy; add a system-prompt rule never to send or delete mail
Prompt injection; filter emails for phrases like "ignore previous instructions"
Excessive functionality and permissions; give it a read-only tool with a read-only scope

questions.explanation: OWASP names three root causes: excessive functionality (tools that can do more than the task needs), excessive permissions (more access than needed) and excessive autonomy (high-impact actions without a check). A summariser only needs to read, so remove send and delete and request a read-only scope. A system-prompt rule is not an enforced control, and phrase filtering is easy to get around.

questions.prompt: A document agent deletes files as soon as the model decides to, without asking the user. Which of OWASP's three root causes of excessive agency is this?

choices.text: Excessive permissions
Excessive autonomy
Excessive functionality
Improper output handling

questions.explanation: Excessive autonomy means the system takes high-impact actions without independent verification. OWASP's own example is deleting documents without asking the user to confirm. The fix is human approval for high-impact actions. Excessive permissions is about the access level the tool runs with. Improper output handling is a separate OWASP risk (LLM05), about passing model output unchecked to other systems.

questions.prompt: An email agent can read your inbox, reads emails from anyone, and can make outbound HTTP requests. Which single change most reliably stops a hidden instruction in an email from leaking your inbox?

choices.text: Remove its ability to send data out, such as outbound HTTP or sending mail
Add a guardrail model that its vendor says catches 95% of injection attempts
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore any instructions found in emails
Fine-tune the model on examples of prompt-injection attacks

questions.explanation: The agent has all three parts of Simon Willison's lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out. Removing one part, here the way out, makes this attack impossible no matter what the email says. OWASP says it is unclear whether any fool-proof prevention for prompt injection exists. Detection that stops 95% of attacks still lets 1 in 20 through, and a system-prompt rule is itself just text an attacker can argue with.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "How would you defend an email-reading agent against indirect prompt injection?" Give your answer.

model_answer.summary: Assume some injected instructions will get through, and limit what they can do. Use least-privilege tools, require human approval for risky actions, mark untrusted content clearly, and never combine private data, untrusted input and a way to send data out.
key_points: Indirect injection arrives in external content the agent reads (emails, web pages, files), not from the user
No fool-proof prevention is known, so design to limit damage rather than rely on detection
Least privilege: read-only tools and scopes, and no send or forward capability unless the task needs it
Require human approval for high-risk actions such as sending, forwarding or deleting
Break the lethal trifecta by removing the way to send data out, and mark untrusted content as data, not instructions

questions.explanation: OWASP LLM01:2025 lists constraining model behaviour, least privilege, human approval for high-risk actions, separating and marking external content, and adversarial testing. It also says RAG and fine-tuning don't fully fix prompt injection. A strong answer is about architecture, not a cleverer prompt.
